title: The Tantalizing Possibility Of Locating Consciousness In The Brain | NOEMA
gist: An MIT Lincoln Laboratory scientist argues that large language models have accidentally falsified neuroscience's core assumption that consciousness requires higher cognition: chatbots now display language, abstraction and social inference with no biological neurons, yet explain nothing about subjective experience. He proposes consciousness lives not in the cortex but in evolutionarily ancient deep-brain structures (upper brainstem, hypothalamus) where feelings function as the common currency for arbitrating competing biological drives — a thesis that would shrink the search for the neural basis of consciousness from the sprawling cortex to a small, anatomically discrete target reachable by tools like non-invasive transcranial/deep-brain stimulation.

themes.theme: LLMs as an accidental falsification of cognitive neuroscience

insights.claim: Modern chatbots demonstrate language, abstraction, social inference and humor without any biological neurons, undermining decades of neuroscience organized around the premise that these abilities were the hard, distinctively biological part of the mind.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The framing that intelligence is 'solved' while consciousness is untouched is becoming the elite scientific consensus — it reframes AI capability debates and points research money at neurotech, not at scaling cognition.
insights.quote: But what few anticipated was that such complex behavior could emerge in the complete absence of biological neurons.
insights.locator: How can this computer seem so very human?

insights.claim: Intelligence may be fully substrate-independent: the same computational architecture that runs in biological neurons can be implemented in silicon microprocessors or even hypothetical mechanical systems of springs, gears and levers, with the physical substrate varying but the behavior-producing computations unchanged.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Substrate-independence of cognition is the intellectual license for compute-centric AI investment; it also implies no moral/regulatory brake on silicon intelligence arises from 'it isn't biological'.
insights.quote: The physical substrate may vary, but the computations, which produce human-like behavior, do not.
insights.locator: A strange possibility has emerged

insights.claim: The author explicitly breaks with the mainstream neuroscience position that cognition is a necessary ingredient of consciousness, arguing that machines now achieving cognitive feats have brought us no closer to understanding conscious awareness.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: If cognition and consciousness decouple, the AI-sentience debate loses its main evidentiary hook — relevant to how policymakers and labs treat model welfare and 'conscious AI' claims.
insights.quote: The mainstream position in neuroscience is that cognition is a necessary ingredient of consciousness
insights.locator: The mainstream position in neuroscience

insights.claim: The genuinely open question is not whether machines can experience anything but what kind of phenomenon consciousness is if it turns out to be unrelated to higher cognition — a reframing that redirects the entire research agenda away from AI-sentience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Watch for funding and talent rotating from 'AI consciousness' philosophy toward mechanistic subcortical neuroscience and the instrumentation that serves it.
insights.quote: But maybe the real mystery is: If consciousness is not fundamentally related to higher cognition, then what kind of phenomenon is it?
insights.locator: Most discussions of AI and consciousness

themes.theme: Feelings as the machinery of rational decision-making

insights.claim: A widely cited Antonio Damasio patient with damage to a prefrontal cortex region critical for emotional valuation retained full reasoning ability yet was paralyzed for hours choosing between two appointment times, showing that decision-making fails when emotional value signals are removed even with intelligence intact.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The clinical precedent for 'valuation is separate from reasoning' — a direct analogue to why purely cognitive AI systems may be capable yet unable to prioritize or choose.
insights.quote: The patient lost the gut feeling that normally guides decision-making.
insights.locator: One of Damasio’s most cited patients

insights.claim: Damasio's 1994 book 'Descartes' Error' established that feelings are not peripheral to rational thought but are part of the machinery that makes rational thought possible.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A three-decade-old framework now being retrofitted as the foundation for post-LLM consciousness research; useful lens for evaluating agentic AI architectures that lack any valuation layer.
insights.quote: Feelings aren’t peripheral to rational thought. They are part of the machinery that makes rational thought possible.
insights.locator: This observation became the foundation

insights.claim: A growing group of researchers now argues that human thought is not a separate category of experience from feeling — the stream of thought may emerge from combinations of a finite number of primitive feeling states, with the brain's actual computations remaining hidden from awareness.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: If experience is a compressed readout rather than the computation, introspection-based methods (and human-report-based AI evals) are measuring the dashboard, not the engine.
insights.locator: Inspired by Damasio’s insights

insights.claim: The author uses LLMs as the explanatory analogy for consciousness: users see returned text but never the trillions of underlying calculations, and subjective experience may likewise be a compressed summary of vast subconscious cortical computation — an aircraft instrument panel for systems too complex to inspect directly.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Notable directional flip: AI is now supplying the metaphors that shape neuroscience theory, not the reverse — a leading indicator of AI's reach into adjacent scientific fields.
insights.quote: Subjective experience may be like the instrument panel of an aircraft, summarizing critical information from systems too complex to inspect directly.
insights.locator: Something similar may happen when the brain

themes.theme: Combinatorial phenomenology: the octillion-state experience space

insights.claim: The author proposes an engineering approach to consciousness — start from the simplest building blocks (hunger, pain, unease, familiarity, anticipation, confidence each having distinctive phenomenology) and ask how they combine, rather than attacking the most complicated component first.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A tractable, testable decomposition is what turns a philosophy problem into a fundable lab program with measurable milestones.
insights.quote: Engineers attempting to understand a complex machine generally don’t begin with the most complicated component.
insights.locator: An Engineering Perspective

insights.claim: Complex thoughts may be assembled from primitive felt states like recipes — two parts familiarity plus one part coherence yielding 'understanding', three parts anticipation plus one part motivation yielding 'hope' — with concepts like a bicycle occupying a distinct location in a multidimensional experiential landscape.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: This is effectively an embedding-space theory of qualia; it implies feeling-state dimensions could eventually be measured, indexed and targeted therapeutically.
insights.quote: Let’s say that two parts familiarity and one part coherence produce the thing we call “understanding.”
insights.locator: Now suppose that complex thoughts are assembled

insights.claim: If conscious experience is built from 30 independent experiential dimensions at eight distinguishable levels each, the space contains roughly 1 octillion (10^27) configurations, while all humans who ever lived — sampling a new conscious state three times per second for entire lifetimes — would collectively cover only about 1 sextillion (10^21), or one-millionth of the landscape.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The quantified claim that human phenomenology is vastly under-explored is the intellectual predicate for psychedelic, neuromodulation and BCI ventures selling access to novel mental states.
insights.quote: Even across the entire history of our species, we would have explored only one-millionth of the available experiential landscape.
insights.locator: Imagine that conscious experience is built from 30

insights.claim: The richness of human thought does not require an endless catalogue of irreducible mental states; it can arise from an enormous combinatorial space built from a small set of primitive feelings.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A small basis set is enumerable and mappable — the difference between an intractable problem and a decade-scale research roadmap.
insights.locator: From this perspective, the richness of human thought

themes.theme: Relocating consciousness from cortex to subcortex

insights.claim: Asked where subjective experience lives, most neuroscientists still point to frontal cerebral cortex, but the author frames this as pre-AI thinking that is now weakening in favor of evolutionarily older deep-brain structures.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A consensus shift in target anatomy would redirect neurotech R&D from cortical surface arrays toward deep-brain access — a different engineering and regulatory problem entirely.
insights.quote: Of course, the idea that consciousness requires intelligence might be pre-AI thinking.
insights.locator: Can Consciousness Be Localized?

insights.claim: Physiologists surgically removed the cerebral cortices from dozens of cats beginning in the 1920s, and genetically modified mice born without cortices have since replicated the result: the animals could eat, reproduce, swim, groom and learn simple mazes despite extreme impairment.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A century-old empirical base that consciousness research can build on immediately — evidence, not conjecture, that cortex is not required for functional behavior.
insights.quote: They could eat, reproduce, swim, groom themselves and even learn simple mazes.
insights.locator: Beginning in the 1920s, physiologists

insights.claim: Deep-brain stimulation in humans can evoke intense subjective experiences while stimulation of large regions of prefrontal cortex often produces little or no conscious effect — a direct asymmetry supporting a subcortical seat of experience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The single most testable empirical asymmetry in the piece, and the one that most directly validates deep-brain stimulation platforms as consciousness research instruments.
insights.locator: This possibility is consistent with the finding

insights.claim: Deep-brain circuits predate the cortex and leave a shared subcortical blueprint across all vertebrates, implying that if consciousness arose early in evolution it still depends on those ancient structures today, from fish to humans.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A conserved vertebrate substrate means animal models translate — cheaper, faster experimental iteration than cortex-focused human work.
insights.locator: It also fits with evolutionary history

insights.claim: Deep-brain structures are more anatomically discrete than sprawling cortical networks, so relocating consciousness there converts the search from an expansive landscape into a relatively small piece of neural anatomy — a discovery the author calls as consequential as any in science.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: This is the core investable claim: a small, discrete target is what makes precision neuromodulation commercially and clinically addressable.
insights.quote: Few discoveries would be more consequential than identifying the specific neural structures responsible for subjective experience.
insights.locator: Here is where it gets especially interesting

insights.claim: The instrument-panel metaphor taken literally implies consciousness is an epiphenomenon — a passive observer with no influence over behavior — which is hard to reconcile with evolution's efficiency at eliminating functions that do not improve survival.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The author names and confronts the strongest objection to his own framework rather than dodging it — a marker of a theory built to be tested rather than sold.
insights.quote: Instrument panels do not fly airplanes; they simply report what the underlying machinery is doing.
insights.locator: Why Feelings Exist

insights.claim: The author's resolution is that feelings are the brain's mechanism for arbitrating competing biological priorities — eat or flee, drink or reproduce, rest or explore — with evolution converting incomparable physiological variables into a common language of subjective feeling rather than comparing them directly.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A concrete functional role for qualia that maps directly onto the reward/objective-arbitration problem in agentic AI — the same architectural gap in systems juggling incompatible goals.
insights.quote: Feelings are not merely reports about the state of the organism; they are the mechanism through which motivation arbitration takes place.
insights.locator: The apparent contradiction disappears

insights.claim: The upper brainstem and hypothalamus are named as the structures ideally positioned to perform motivational arbitration, making them the concrete anatomical candidates for the seat of subjective experience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Named targets are what stimulation and imaging companies build around — watch which structures the next generation of non-invasive neuromodulation trials actually address.
insights.locator: The ancient structures of the upper brainstem

insights.claim: The cortex did not replace ancient deep-brain architecture but feeds it richer information through descending projections, so — paraphrasing neuroscientist Bjorn Merker — the cortex may generate the contents of consciousness while deep-brain structures generate conscious experience itself.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The cleanest division-of-labor formulation in the essay, and the one most likely to become the field's shorthand if the subcortical thesis gains ground.
insights.quote: the cortex may generate the contents of consciousness, while deep-brain structures generate conscious experience itself
insights.locator: To paraphrase neuroscientist Bjorn Merker

insights.claim: The author concedes a hard open problem: whatever physical mechanism gives rise to feeling must also influence action-selection circuits, but that interaction cannot be deciphered while we still do not know how brain activity creates feeling in the first place.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The explicit bottleneck to watch — progress here, not on scaling models, is what would signal the field is actually converging.
insights.locator: If this picture is correct, whatever physical mechanisms

themes.theme: Field fragmentation and MIT's institutional bet

insights.claim: Consciousness research has not converged on a common framework for evaluating competing ideas, so researchers disagree not only about the answer but about the question itself — meaning that convincing the field of a discovery may prove almost as difficult as making it.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Pre-paradigmatic fields absorb capital slowly and produce contested results; expect long validation cycles before any commercializable neurotech claim is settled.
insights.quote: Researchers disagree not only about the answer, but about the question itself.
insights.locator: Bringing Consciousness Research Into Mainstream Neuroscience

insights.claim: MIT hosts an unusually broad and unconsolidated cluster of relevant work — Emery Brown on anesthesia-driven loss and return of consciousness, Earl Miller on cortical dynamics, philosopher Matthias Michel on conceptual foundations, Ed Boyden on circuit recording and manipulation tools, Fan Wang on pain and aversive circuits, Josh Tenenbaum on computational principles of cognition, and Satrajit Ghosh on AI tools for large neurophysiological datasets — yet few of them self-identify as consciousness scientists.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A concrete map of where the talent and tooling already sit; MIT's interdisciplinary consciousness initiative is the vehicle that could consolidate it, and these labs are the spinout pipeline to track.
insights.locator: Among scientists here at MIT

insights.claim: Neuroscientists can spend entire careers mapping circuits for pain, fear, memory or decision-making on solid scientific ground, but the moment they ask how those circuits give rise to subjective experience the ground becomes shaky and they find themselves steeped in conjecture.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: The career-risk barrier explains why the field is under-invested relative to its potential payoff — and why institutional cover from a place like MIT is the unlock.
insights.quote: But the moment they ask how those circuits give rise to subjective experience, the scientific ground becomes shaky.
insights.locator: This creates an unusual situation

insights.claim: The author predicts the boundary between consciousness research and mainstream neuroscience will gradually dissolve as theories become grounded in testable neural mechanisms, singling out non-invasive deep-brain stimulation as the enabling technology.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Non-invasive deep-brain access — the author's own transcranial ultrasound specialty — is the specific instrumentation category that benefits if this thesis wins.
insights.quote: As theories become more firmly grounded in testable neural mechanisms, such as with non-invasive deep-brain stimulation, the boundary between consciousness research and mainstream neuroscience may gradually dissolve.
insights.locator: This situation may be changing

insights.claim: Artificial neural networks, originally inspired by the cerebral cortex, have become indispensable partners in consciousness research by extracting patterns from neural data that would have been difficult to recognize only a decade ago.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: AI as scientific instrument rather than subject — the recurring pattern of AI compounding into adjacent research verticals and pulling their timelines forward.
insights.quote: Artificial neural networks, originally inspired by the cerebral cortex, have become indispensable partners in that effort
insights.locator: The Search Continues

insights.claim: The author states the binding constraint on progress is not ideas but resources — the time, talent and funding needed to convert decades of descriptive observation into mechanistic explanation and to build a community that treats consciousness as central neuroscience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: An explicit capital-and-talent ask from an MIT Lincoln Laboratory scientist — read as an early signal of an emerging funding category around mechanistic consciousness research.
insights.quote: The work ahead will require more than good ideas.
insights.locator: The work ahead will require more
